newsitem.title: USA: Critics say Clinton shuns tough Mideast line.
newsitem.headline: Critics say Clinton shuns tough Mideast line.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's apparent failure to wring concessions from Israel as he tries to revive Middle East peace talks exposes his weak position in a pro-Israeli domestic political climate, analysts say.

Critics charge that fear of offending politically powerful -- and wealthy -- lobby groups that back the Jewish state has prevented Clinton from taking the tough moves necessary to rescue the peace process from its current crisis.

Administration officials respond that they are even-handed mediators between Israel and the Palestinians, and that it is up to the parties -- not the United States -- to resolve their problems for themselves.
Clinton himself has made that point repeatedly but, at a news conference on Tuesday, he nonetheless rejected a suggestion the United States was losing influence over Israel.

"I wouldn't assume that based on the comments that have been made so far," he said, adding: "I would not conclude from the fact that I'm giving very noncommittal answers that we cannot get it (the Middle East peace process) going again. I think there's a fairly decent chance that we can."
But he did not elaborate on the basis for his optimism, and U.S. newspapers on Tuesday trumpeted failure for his talks on Monday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The meeting "fails to jump-start peace negotiations", headlined the Washington Post, while the New York Times said that "no Mideast progress is reported".

Clinton's aides said he had offered Netanyahu unspecified ideas for breaking the deadlock sparked by Israel's launch of a Jewish housing project in mainly Arab East Jerusalem last month. The ideas would also be put to the Palestinians later this week, they said.
The administration signalled the contentiousness of the talks with Netanyahu by labeling them "frank" and "candid" instead of the usual "constructive" or "useful".
But some foreign policy experts said Clinton had passed up a chance to press the right-wing Likud leader to halt the housing project, which has enraged Palestinians.

"I think they (U.S. leaders) have made a clear decision that they're not prepared to be tough with Israel," said Judith Kipper, Middle East analyst at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
"There is a serious domestic concern here."

Columnists Rowland Evans and Robert Novak went further, saying Clinton had "blinked away the prospect of applying U.S. power" to make Netanyahu back down, a failure that "risks a mini-war on the West Bank and terror inside Israel".
The widely-read commentators quoted "a key American diplomat" as saying the president and his aides were reluctant to pressure Israel because "that could cost the Democrats precious campaign funds".

While Clinton at first criticised the Israeli decision to go ahead with the housing project in Jerusalem, the subsequent U.S. veto of a U.N. Security Council resolution condemning the plan sent a contradictory signal, critics say.
Administration officials, however, portray U.S. policies as balanced and statesmanlike, befitting the U.S. role as honest broker in Israeli-Palestinian talks.

Although the former administration of George Bush once witheld $10 billion in loan guarantees to Israel because of Israeli settlement policies, U.S. officials say the start of direct talks since then makes such gestures impossible now.
The fact remains that no major meeting of a Jewish organisation goes by without an administration official reaffirming the close bonds between America and Israel.

On the eve of the Clinton-Netanyahu talks, Vice-President Al Gore, expected to run for president in 2000, told the American-Israel Public Affair Committee: "We will never permit anyone to drive a wedge between the United States and Israel."

And, whatever the truth of what passed between Clinton and Netanyahu, the Israeli leader told the same group later that "we have a sure friend in the White House -- actually two friends, the president and the vice president".
The importance of pro-Israel lobby groups to presidential contenders aside, the administration also faces a Republican-dominated Congress broadly sympathetic to Israel.

A strong current of opinion in the legislature, going well beyond members beholden to a Jewish vote, holds that Israel continues to be an island of Western-style democracy beleaguered by terrorists and hostile Arab dictatorships.
The State Department may have concluded that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has made the transition from guerrilla leader to statesman. Many in Congress see it differently.
